para.a: Lots of newspapers and TV channels talked about the fire.
Advertisers try to sell things to a certain group of people.
para.b: Advertisers design their campaigns to appeal to a specific *target audience*.

para.a: Many people today buy too many things they do not need.
para.b: Modern society is increasingly shaped by *consumerism*.

p1.q: How do you usually get the news?
p1.a: Mostly through my phone, to be honest. I follow a couple of reliable news apps, and I sometimes watch the evening *broadcast* with my parents. I try to avoid getting news from *social media* because it isn't always accurate.

p1.q: Do you pay attention to advertisements?
p1.a: Not really. I usually skip *commercials* on video sites as soon as I can. However, I must admit that a clever *slogan* sometimes stays in my head for days, so I suppose they work on me more than I think.

Yes, very much. I particularly like *documentaries* about nature and history because I learn something new every time. Last month I watched one about coral reefs, and it made me much more aware of how fragile the oceans are.

p2.cue: Describe an advertisement that you remember well.
points: and explain why you remember it so well
p2.a: I'd like to talk about an *advertisement* for a bottled water company that I saw a few years ago. I first noticed it on television during a football match, but later it appeared all over *social media* as well. The *commercial* began with a young boy in a hot, dry village walking a long way to collect water for his family. Then the scene changed to a group of volunteers building a well, and the boy's face lit up when clean water came out. At the end, a simple *slogan* appeared: 'Every bottle helps one more child.' The company promised to donate part of its profits to water projects. I remember it so well because it did not try to *persuade* me with famous faces or loud music. Instead, it told a real human story. Of course, I know it was still a marketing strategy to improve the *brand*, but I felt it had a positive message, and I actually switched to that brand of water afterwards.

p3.q: Do you think advertising aimed at children should be restricted?
p3.a: Yes, I believe it should be, at least to some extent. Young children cannot easily tell the difference between entertainment and an advert, so they are easily *misled*. Many countries already limit adverts for unhealthy food during children's programmes, and I think that is sensible. Parents should still teach children to think critically, but the law can offer extra protection.

p3.q: How has social media changed the way people get the news?
p3.a: It has changed things enormously. In the past, people relied on a few newspapers and television channels, whereas now anyone can share a story within seconds. This is positive because news spreads faster, but it also means that *fake news* can go *viral* before anyone checks it. As a result, I think people need better media literacy skills than ever before.

writing.q: Some people think that advertising has a negative effect on society because it encourages people to buy things they do not need. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
essay: Advertising is everywhere in modern life, from roadside billboards to the *social media* feeds on our phones. Some people argue that it harms society by encouraging people to buy products they do not really need. While I accept that advertising has some benefits, I largely agree that its overall effect is negative.

The main problem is that advertising fuels *consumerism*. Companies spend enormous sums designing *commercials* that link their *brand* to happiness, success or popularity, so that consumers feel incomplete without the latest phone or pair of trainers. Increasingly, *influencers* promote products in a way that looks like personal advice rather than marketing, which makes it even harder for young people to resist. As a result, many families spend beyond their means and fall into debt, while the constant demand for new goods creates huge amounts of waste.

Furthermore, some advertisers deliberately *mislead* the public. Food companies, for example, may describe sugary cereals as healthy simply because vitamins have been added, and young viewers, who are often the *target audience* for such products, cannot easily see through these claims. On the other hand, it is true that advertising informs consumers about new products and pays for much of the free content we enjoy online. However, these benefits could be preserved through stricter regulation rather than by allowing companies to *persuade* people without limits.

In conclusion, although advertising plays a useful role in the economy, I believe it does more harm than good because it promotes excessive spending and often relies on misleading messages. Governments should therefore set clearer rules, particularly for advertising aimed at children.
